new_statements.quote: Dazu gehört besonders die sorgfältige Beobachtung der Töne im Einzelwort. Nun sind aber Ewe und Haussa Tonsprachen verschiedenen Grades. [...] muß man das Haussa ähnlich wie das Twi als grammatische Tonsprache ansehen, d. h. der Ton wechselt im Einzelwort, besonders im Verbum, nach Maßgabe der grammatischen Funktion. [...] Dieser grammatische Ton wird von FOLI ignoriert, das Verbum erhält fälschlich einen festen Ton, offenbar wie der dem Sprecher von einer vielgebrauchten Form her in Erinnerung geblieben ist. [...] Wieweit er Eigenarten seiner Satztongebung auf den Satzton des Haussa überträgt, muß noch untersucht werden.
new_statements.translation: This includes in particular the careful observance of the tones in the individual word. But Ewe and Hausa are tone languages of different degrees. [...] Hausa, like Twi, must be regarded as a grammatical tone language, i.e. the tone changes within the individual word, especially in the verb, according to grammatical function. [...] This grammatical tone is ignored by FOLI; the verb wrongly receives a fixed tone, evidently the one that stayed in the speaker's memory from some frequently used form. [...] To what extent he transfers peculiarities of his own sentence-tone to Hausa sentence tone remains to be investigated.
new_statements.citation: Feyer, Ursula (1947). Haussa als Verkehrssprache. Zeitschrift für Phonetik und allgemeine Sprachwissenschaft 1(3): 108-129.
new_statements.locator: pp. 123-124 (concluding section; pp. 39-40); see also section 'Die Töne', pp. 110-111 (pp. 26-27)

new_statements.rule_in_words: The variety is treated as tonal (high, low, rising, falling tones marked, p. 110): lexical word tones are kept carefully and stably by the speaker, while Hausa grammatical (verbal) tone alternations are levelled to a fixed tone per verb. Word stress/accent is never mentioned; no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: Speaker has rising tones where Bargery's standard Hausa has low or high (p. 111), interpreted as contractions or dialectal relics; verbs lose grammatical tone patterns (pp. 111, 124).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Töne im Einzelwort'); sentence intonation explicitly left uninvestigated. Data are elicited words and texts from a single speaker recorded in Berlin. IDENTITY CAVEAT: the variety is the trade Hausa of an Ewe speaker from SE Togo (itinerant-trader Hausa of Togo/Dahomey/Gold Coast), not the Gibanawa of Jega, Nigeria.
new_statements.identity_note: The only description Glottolog ever attached to giba1240, Feyer 1947, describes the trade Hausa ('Verkehrshaussa') of a single Ewe informant, Bonifatius Foli (b. 1877, SE Togo, d. Berlin 1947), i.e. the itinerant-trader Hausa of Togo/Dahomey/Gold Coast — not the Gibanawa contact language of Jega LGA, Kebbi State, Nigeria (Ethnologue: 'Gembanawa, Gimbanawa, Jega'). Glottolog 5.3 has since dropped Feyer from giba1240 and now lists only Ethnologue 28. No dedicated description of Gibanawa proper exists in any source found; Feyer's tone statements should not be entered as Gibanawa data. A closer Glottolog match for Feyer's variety would be Hausa proper (haus1257) as an L2 trader variety; no separate glottocode exists for West-African trader Hausa.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. The article describes the trade Hausa of one Ewe speaker from SE Togo (Bonifatius Foli), not Jega Gibanawa. Section 'Die Töne' (p. 110-111): the speaker observes lexical tones carefully and consistently, even has rising tones; summary pp. 123-124: Hausa is a grammatical tone language, but Foli ignores grammatical tone and gives verbs a fixed tone; sentence intonation left for later study.
